items.readable_text:
Content:
Given a real interval [MATH: D = (a,b)\subset \mathbb R,] the length of this interval can be represented by the integral

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Length}(D) = \int_a^b \,\textrm d x]

Content:
which we can also write as

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Length}(D) = \int\limits_D \,\textrm d x.]

Content:
Suppose we define an invertible function [MATH: u = u(x).] By the change of variables formula, the length of our interval can also be expressed as

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Length}(D) = \int\limits_{\Delta} \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}\, \textrm d u.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- Whenever we perform a change of variables, the domain of integration changes, too. This new integration domain is denoted [MATH: \Delta.] More technically, [MATH: \Delta] is the image of the [MATH: D] under the action of [MATH: u(x).]
- If we think of [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}] as a fraction, the [MATH: \textrm d u]'s in our length formula appear to "cancel out," leaving only the original [MATH: \textrm d x.] This makes the change of variables formula easy to remember.

Content:
So, to summarize,

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Length}(D) = \int\limits_D \,\textrm d x = \int\limits_{\Delta} \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}\, \textrm d u.]

Content:
Since the length of our interval is simply [MATH: b-a,] it's doubtful that we'll ever use this formula in practice! However, it does indicate how we might use a change of variables to find the area of a complex region in two-dimensional space. Let's explore this idea in more detail.

Content:
Consider the region [MATH: D] in the [MATH: xy]-plane shown above. The area of this region is given by

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x\textrm d y]

Content:
where we'll use the convention [MATH: \textrm d A = \mathrm d x\textrm d y] when referring to integration with respect to the Cartesian coordinates [MATH: x] and [MATH: y.]

Content:
This region looks pretty complicated. In such cases, it's often easier to find an invertible transformation [MATH: \mathbf T] (i.e., change of variables) whose inverse maps the region [MATH: D] to simpler, preferably rectangular, region [MATH: \Delta] in the [MATH: uv]-plane.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/33c69e4c15b46f222ec5d5226a8bbf3d]

Content:
So, rather than computing the required area by integrating with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] we can instead perform the transformation and integrate with respect to [MATH: u] and [MATH: v.]

Content:
To carry out this process, we apply the change of variables formula

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Area}(D) = \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v]

Content:
where [MATH: \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}] is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to [MATH: \mathbf T.]

Content:
Notice that this formula is analogous to the one we saw earlier for computing the length of an interval. In particular:

Content:
- If we consider the Jacobian as a kind of fraction, the [MATH: \partial(u,v)] and [MATH: \textrm d u\textrm d v] parts appear to "cancel out," similar to the previous formula.
- Note that [MATH: \mathbf T] could be orientation-reversing. We take the absolute value of the Jacobian to ensure that [MATH: D] and [MATH: \Delta] have the same orientation.

Content:
Finally, note that the change of variables formula assumes that [MATH: \mathbf T] is a [MATH: C^1] transformation and has no critical points in the interior of [MATH: \Delta.]

Content:

In other words, we require a change of variables that reduces the equations of our curves to something like the following:
[MATH: u = \textrm{const}_1, \quad
u = \textrm{const}_2, \quad

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Given a real interval [MATH: D = (a,b)\subset \mathbb R,] the length of this interval can be represented by the integral

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Length}(D) = \int_a^b \,\textrm d x]

Content:
which we can also write as

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Length}(D) = \int\limits_D \,\textrm d x.]

Content:
Suppose we define an invertible function [MATH: u = u(x).] By the change of variables formula, the length of our interval can also be expressed as

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Length}(D) = \int\limits_{\Delta} \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}\, \textrm d u.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- Whenever we perform a change of variables, the domain of integration changes, too. This new integration domain is denoted [MATH: \Delta.] More technically, [MATH: \Delta] is the image of the [MATH: D] under the action of [MATH: u(x).]
- If we think of [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}] as a fraction, the [MATH: \textrm d u]'s in our length formula appear to "cancel out," leaving only the original [MATH: \textrm d x.] This makes the change of variables formula easy to remember.

Content:
So, to summarize,

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Length}(D) = \int\limits_D \,\textrm d x = \int\limits_{\Delta} \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}\, \textrm d u.]

Content:
Since the length of our interval is simply [MATH: b-a,] it's doubtful that we'll ever use this formula in practice! However, it does indicate how we might use a change of variables to find the area of a complex region in two-dimensional space. Let's explore this idea in more detail.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Change of Variables Formula

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8267812ac0a59ca3430c5ebaeef0f80b]

Content:
Consider the region [MATH: D] in the [MATH: xy]-plane shown above. The area of this region is given by

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x\textrm d y]

Content:
where we'll use the convention [MATH: \textrm d A = \mathrm d x\textrm d y] when referring to integration with respect to the Cartesian coordinates [MATH: x] and [MATH: y.]

Content:
This region looks pretty complicated. In such cases, it's often easier to find an invertible transformation [MATH: \mathbf T] (i.e., change of variables) whose inverse maps the region [MATH: D] to simpler, preferably rectangular, region [MATH: \Delta] in the [MATH: uv]-plane.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/33c69e4c15b46f222ec5d5226a8bbf3d]

Content:
So, rather than computing the required area by integrating with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] we can instead perform the transformation and integrate with respect to [MATH: u] and [MATH: v.]

Content:
To carry out this process, we apply the change of variables formula

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Area}(D) = \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v]

Content:
where [MATH: \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}] is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to [MATH: \mathbf T.]

Content:
Notice that this formula is analogous to the one we saw earlier for computing the length of an interval. In particular:

Content:
- If we consider the Jacobian as a kind of fraction, the [MATH: \partial(u,v)] and [MATH: \textrm d u\textrm d v] parts appear to "cancel out," similar to the previous formula.
- Note that [MATH: \mathbf T] could be orientation-reversing. We take the absolute value of the Jacobian to ensure that [MATH: D] and [MATH: \Delta] have the same orientation.

Content:
Finally, note that the change of variables formula assumes that [MATH: \mathbf T] is a [MATH: C^1] transformation and has no critical points in the interior of [MATH: \Delta.]

Content:
Often, the most challenging part is finding a suitable change of variables. The main idea is to get a nice rectangular shape with sides parallel to the axes in the [MATH: uv]-plane. In other words, we require a change of variables that reduces the equations of our curves to something like the following:
[MATH: u = \textrm{const}_1, \quad
u = \textrm{const}_2, \quad
v = \textrm{const}_3, \quad
v = \textrm{const}_4]

Content:
Let's look at a concrete example of computing an area using the change of variables formula.

---

Item 3 — Tutorial: A Worked Example

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/19c29b32cce18d8d29708037505220c5]

Content:
Consider the finite region [MATH: D] in the first quadrant (shown above) bounded by the lines

Content:
[MATH: {\color{blue}{3y-x}} = 3, \qquad {\color{blue}{3y-x}} = 6, \qquad {\color{red}{2x+y}}=4, \qquad {\color{red}{2x+y}}=6.]

The area of the required region is given by

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y.]

Content:
[MATH: [u; v]]

Content:
This transformation maps some region [MATH: \Delta] in the [MATH: uv]-plane to our region [MATH: D] in the [MATH: xy]-plane.

Content:
To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right| \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v]
where [MATH: \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}] is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to [MATH: \mathbf T.]

Content:
Looking at the lines that bound our region, we consider the following change of variables:

Content:
[MATH: u = {\color{blue}{3y-x}}, \qquad v = {\color{red}{2x+y}}]

Content:
Note that this change of variables gives us the inverse function [MATH: \mathbf T^{-1},] that is

Content:
[MATH: [x; y]]

[MATH: 2x + y = 4|⟹|v = 4; 2x + y = 6|⟹|v = 6]

Therefore, our domain in the [MATH: uv]-plane is the following rectangle:

Content:
[MATH: \Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 3 \leq u \leq 6, \quad 4 \leq v \leq 6\big\}]

[IMG: /graphics/d4670b752177cbf1a02797c8ad5be4db]

[MATH: u = 3y-x, \qquad v = 2x+y.]

Content:
Step 3: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to [MATH: \mathbf T.]

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to [MATH: \mathbf T] is
[MATH: \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = -\dfrac17.]
Note that [MATH: \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0] everywhere inside [MATH: \Delta.] In other words, [MATH: \mathbf T] has no critical points inside [MATH: \Delta.]

Step 4: Compute the required area.
